issues.claim: Finding 7 ("A documented LinkedIn outbound funnel produced 2 paying clients from 487 connection requests in 30 days") is rated strength "Medium".
issues.problem: The source is a single self-published founder blog post. The brief itself rates the other finding drawn from the same post (finding 8, the free-pilot economics) as "Low", and the role standard treats single-founder anecdotes as Low. Rating the same 30-day anecdote Medium overstates it, and the recommendations are built on it.
issues.fix: Downgrade finding 7 to "Low" and say explicitly that the funnel is one founder's 30-day sample with no external verification (submit.co, which indexes the same post, likewise notes it hasn't checked founders' numbers).

issues.claim: Recommendation 2: "roughly 100 targeted LinkedIn touches per held call, ~2 held calls per signed pilot, and about 1 paying client per 2 pilots. For 3 clients, plan ~300-500 targeted touches and 6+ pilots over 2-3 months".
issues.problem: The arithmetic is inconsistent with the cited case and with its own per-unit rates. The source funnel is 487 connection requests to 8 held calls (~61 touches per held call, not ~100) and 487 requests to 2 paying clients. Walking the brief's own rates: 3 clients = 6 pilots = ~12 held calls = ~730 touches at 61 per call (or ~1,200 at its stated 100 per call). "300-500 touches" understates the documented effort by roughly 2x and is lower than the single case that produced only 2 clients.
issues.fix: Restate as ~60-100 touches per held call, ~1 paying client per 2 pilots, and ~700-1,200 touches (roughly 500 per paying client) for 3 clients over 2-3 months; or drop the touch count and keep only the pilot/call ratios.

issues.claim: Resources: Hinge buyer studies "with sample sizes stated (822 buyers/533 providers; 1,028 buyers; 1,914 buyers/3,160 sellers for the 4th edition)".
issues.problem: The 822/533 and 1,028 figures are on the two cited pages. The 1,914 buyers/3,160 sellers figure is not on either cited page; it appears in Hinge's "Inside the Buyer's Brain" 2022 webinar deck (https://hingemarketing.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/IBB-Webinar-2022.pdf), which I opened and confirmed. The Hinge executive-summary page that would normally carry it returns HTTP 403.
issues.fix: Add the webinar-PDF URL beside the 1,914/3,160 figure, or delete that figure from the resource entry.

issues.problem: The page is undated and carries no publication year. The interview references "last month, in January" and "right now in February", which is consistent with either 2025 or 2026, so the 2025 label is unsupported as stated.
issues.fix: Mark the year as "undated (interview references January/February, year not stated)" rather than 2025.

issues.claim: Strength ratings are internally inconsistent across vendor sources: finding 6 (Belkins/TNW cold-email benchmark) is "Medium" while finding 12 (Thryv vendor survey) is "Low".
issues.problem: Both are vendor-published material. The Belkins benchmark is a large dataset (7.5M emails) but is delivered as a Belkins-authored op-ed on a news site, i.e. vendor marketing with a self-reported methodology; the brief gives no reason for treating it as stronger than the other vendor source.
issues.fix: Either rate finding 6 "Low-Medium" with a note that the dataset is large but self-reported by a lead-gen vendor with no independent audit, or explain in the evidence line why the sample size lifts it above Thryv.

claims_checked.claim: Mixology 2025 B2B Buyer Report: 511 B2B buyers, 48% US / 52% UK; research start search engines 40%, peer recommendations 19%, events 15%, LinkedIn 9%, vendor websites 6%.
58% of buyers use peer recommendations at some point versus 19% who start there; evaluation uses reviews 68%, demos/trials 65%, peer recommendations 58%, case studies 54%.

Case studies the most influential content type (42%), ahead of pricing/ROI calculators (18%) and webinars/video demos (18%); credibility from reputation 45%, content 21%, testimonials 21%, certifications/awards 3%.

Frustrations: lack of clear pricing 69%, persistent follow-ups 63%, slow response 61%, poor understanding of needs 56%, generic communication 51%; preferred first engagement sales rep 30%, demo/trial 30%, website 20%; under-100-employee firms 31%/29%/25%.
Caveat: Mixology sample 39% under 100 employees and 23% over $100M revenue; report is 55 pages and free.

Hinge: 822 buyers and 533 providers; buyers find a firm by asking another person 71% of the time, online search 11%; cost tipped the decision 8%; reputation most important; 69% very willing to recommend, almost three quarters of the time nobody asked.

Hinge 'Beyond Referrals': 1,028 buyers; over 99% check a firm out, average buyer uses more than three strategies; over 80% visit the website; slightly more likely to search online than ask a friend; references the least-used method; social media used more than contacting references.

Belkins/TNW: 7.5M cold emails in 2025 averaging 0.45% reply; 0.50% H1, 0.40% H2 (20% decline), 0.35% December; larger dataset of 16.5M emails, 20M+ LinkedIn attempts, 5M+ calls; methodology caveat on changing denominators.
Pitfall: Google advises bulk senders to keep user-reported spam rate under 0.1%.

Dietrich funnel: 487 requests, 175 accepted (36%), 43 replies (25% of accepted), 15 interested (35% of replies), 11 calls booked, 8 held (2 cancelled, 1 no-show), 5 second calls, 4 signed, 4 onboarded, 2 pilots finished (2 stopped early), 2 paid clients.

Pilot terms: 'very non-committal and friendly-worded 2-page agreement' for a '1-month free pilot'; each pilot costs '10+ hours of manual setup, scraping costs, and AI credits'; every client driven to results signed the paid plan; 'many unpaid test clients'; high-touch acquisition 'an expensive way to acquire clients'.
Dietrich post year 2025 (30-day window).
Skyvern: list of about 100 people, emailed each, '~30 people replied', 4 agreed to work with them before any product existed, first version shipped over a weekend.
Skyvern story dated June 2025.

Millionaire Copy/Igor: ~1,000 emails a day, ~3 weeks to get the system working, first client ~2 weeks later, second a week after, 11 clients in January, ~$19,000 in three months, ~3,000 emails a week while delivering, tied to a paid AI course (AI campus, $50).
Finding 10 year label 2025.

Census BTOS: Dec 14, 2025 to May 3, 2026; overall use 17-20%; 19.8% as of May 3, 2026; 37% of 250+ firms, 32% of 100-249; no significant change under 20 employees; less than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees; Information 39.7%, Finance & Insurance 33.9%, Retail ~14%; wording revised November 2025; 15-function supplement.

Thryv: 540 US SMB decision-makers, 1-100 employees, $100k-$9.9M revenue, collected May 4-14 2025; 55% using AI (39% in 2024) including software that 'now uses AI'; 68%/53%/37% by size; professional services 71%, restaurant/retail 61%, construction 48%; 80% necessary for new customers; 63% daily; 2.3 business areas; 22-page report.

buildpurdue: 'A paid pilot does not need to be expensive. It needs a price, a decision-maker, a success measure, and an end date. If you cannot name those four things, keep the engagement as discovery or decline it.'; free pilot only when 'you are deliberately buying learning and the cost is capped'; 'a paid engagement with an uncomfortable price conversation delayed'; five-question agreement checklist.
